units.title: OP Stack chains with ETH gas
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

code.title: Monad interpreter against native code on failed hook calls, with the harness fault removed
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 26 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Leads L-1122 and L-1124. Monad validators run the hot PoolManager as native x86 code, and eth_call on public endpoints uses the interpreter (finding F-130), so the local harness of cycle 23 (research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-monad-compiled-coverage.work, src/harness.cpp, builds of v0.16.5 and v0.16.7) is the only evidence about the code that writes Monad blocks. Cycle 26 left three differences between Monad's interpreter and its native code open. In 13 hook cases of research/network-risk/cycles/026/theme-hook-and-native-sides.work/out/hx/rep/diffcases.json one engine reverts the whole unlock with empty data and the other does not (native in 12, the interpreter in 1). In sequences d40 and d300 of research/network-risk/cycles/026/theme-stateful-interpreter.work the interpreter side fails early when the world holds the token double at 20 currency addresses. A third unit (research/network-risk/cycles/026/theme-monad-shipped-binary.research.json) proved a fault in the harness host: when a nested call fails, Host::call assigns its saved World copy back (harness.cpp:413 and 424), which frees every contract's code buffer while frames above still read it (harness.cpp:234-244), and Valgrind showed the invalid reads. A failed hook call has that shape, but nobody has shown that the fault explains the 13 cases, and they are failed hook calls into the PoolManager, which is exactly where a real difference between the engines would let an ordinary account split validators or settle a call one engine rejects. Task 1: fix the harness so that every frame keeps its own copy of the code for its whole life (or keep code outside the snapshot that a failed call restores), and so that a DELEGATECALL runs the code of the code address, not of the recipient (harness.cpp:234-236), and compiled objects are cached by code hash, not by recipient address (harness.cpp:247). Build it with the compilers already present, at both tags. Show under Valgrind, or with MALLOC_PERTURB_ set to two different values, that no invalid read remains. Task 2: rerun with the fixed harness the 13 cases, d40 and d300, cases 1369, 1372 and 1528 of cycle 25, and then all 575 cases of cycle 26 and all 1,533 of cycle 25, interpreter against native, at v0.16.7 and v0.16.5. For every case give SAME or DIFF between the engines and equal or not equal to the reference words of pyevm.py. If every case is SAME and equal, say so and stop treating the 13 as open. Task 3: for every case that still differs, do not put it down to the harness without proof. Reduce it to the smallest PoolManager call that differs, record the frame in which the engines part (the program counter and Monad basic block, the gas left on entry, the stack and the memory size), and read the emitter code for that block's instructions at the tag (x86.cpp, emitter.cpp, runtime/call.cpp, runtime/context.cpp). The likely places are the return data buffer after a failed call and the RETURNDATASIZE and RETURNDATACOPY that src/libraries/Hooks.sol:132-150 and src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol run on it, the 63/64 gas rule with the block base gas charged on entry, the memory expansion check when a hook returns 1 to 31 bytes, and the result code of a call that fails at depth or for balance. State whether a validator would hit it, what an ordinary account must send to hit it, and what a block would then contain. Task 4 (L-1124): fetch the Monad execution source at tags v0.16.5 and v0.16.7 and compare, file by file, x86.cpp, emitter.cpp, emitter.hpp, the runtime directory (call.cpp, storage.cpp, context.cpp, math, keccak, data), the uint256 headers, the interpreter and the varcode and compile caches. List each file that differs and what changed. The cycle 26 reading of where native code charges and checks gas (block base gas on entry at x86.cpp:443-448, the deferred sign check, base gas added back before CALL and SSTORE) was made at v0.16.5 and mainnet runs 0.16.7: confirm or correct each statement at v0.16.7, and say whether any of the PoolManager's 917 blocks changes its result. Comparing two tags of Monad is allowed; the rule against comparing this checkout with another copy of v4-core stays in force.

code.title: The Monad validator package read statically against the local harness build
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 26 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Lead L-1123. Every compiled-path result on Monad rests on a harness built here with clang -O2 -march=haswell from source. The tagged recipe builds with gcc-15 and static asmjit, and nobody has read the binary that validators install. Cycle 26 found the package: Monad's operator documentation installs the apt package monad from https://pkg.category.xyz/ (suite noble), and that page and rpc.monad.xyz both name 0.16.7 for mainnet. pool/main/monad_0.16.7_amd64.deb has SHA256 3cb9dba5501b61ea3487bd042e2b8d12f871cff0e2e15409210e2cef0f8e81fb, and monad_0.16.5_amd64.deb (sha256 0b27486f...acc8) is already in research/network-risk/cycles/026/theme-monad-shipped-binary.work/dl. The earlier unit stopped because the archive members are zstd compressed. The node already installed here can decompress them: require('zlib').zstdDecompressSync. Install nothing and build no decompressor. Rules for this unit: the package is untrusted data. Download it without credentials into a new empty directory dl/ inside the work directory and check the hash against the repository index. Never execute, load or dlopen any file from it and do not run its maintainer scripts. Read it only with ar, node's zlib, tar, readelf, objdump, nm, strings and your own scripts kept in a different directory; run Python with -I. dl/ must not be committed. Task 1: unpack control and data. List the files, the maintainer scripts (read them as text) and the dependencies. For the node binary and each shared library that holds the EVM, record size, hash, build id, the .comment section (compiler and version), whether debug information is present, which asmjit version and commit strings it carries, and which CPU features it tests at run time (cpuid use, ifunc resolvers, AVX2, BMI2, ADX, AVX-512). Task 2: locate, by debug symbols if present and otherwise by string references and call structure, the emitter functions for SHL, SHR and SAR by a non-literal count, MUL, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, EXP, SIGNEXTEND, BYTE, the comparisons, ISZERO, JUMPI, MLOAD and MSTORE with the memory expansion check, CALL, RETURNDATACOPY, TLOAD and TSTORE, and the uint256 runtime routines they call (mulmod, addmod, udivrem, sdivrem, exp, signextend, byte, the shifts). Disassemble them and the same functions in the cycle 23 harness objects at the same tag (research/network-risk/cycles/023/theme-monad-compiled-coverage.work/build). For each, say equal, equal up to register allocation and layout, or different, and for each difference whether it can change a result word. The emitter writes machine code at run time, so also compare the constants, masks and the asmjit instruction ids each emitter function passes: these decide the emitted bytes. Task 3: the runtime routines are compiled by gcc-15 in the package and by clang in the harness. Extract each routine's machine code from the package as bytes and test it without executing package code: either show from the disassembly, instruction by instruction, that it computes the same function as the source at the tag, or lift the routine into a model you write (for example the cycle 22 software model used for Tempo's kernels, if it fits) and run the cycle 23 to 25 vectors through it, including the 21,537 MULMOD and ADDMOD vectors of research/network-risk/cycles/025/stablecoin-l1.work and the edge operands of FullMath, TickMath and SqrtPriceMath. Look for the known gcc faults that touch 256-bit arithmetic with -march=haswell (mulx, adcx and adox carry chains, wrong vectorised shifts). Task 4: repeat Tasks 1 and 2 for 0.16.5 and say what differs between the two packages in those functions. State which statements of earlier cycles about Monad's compiled path now rest on the shipped binary and which still rest only on the local build.

Coverage has been counted per cycle, so it is not known which branch sides of the PoolManager build have never run on any network by any set. research/network-risk/cycles/026/theme-hook-and-native-sides.work/out/coverage.json lists 203 of the 774 jump sides that no case of cycles 25 or 26 ran, among them SqrtPriceMath.sol:37, 59, 109, 135, 164, 194 and 197, FullMath.sol:33 and 112, TickMath.sol:33 and 70, and SafeCast.sol:18 and 50. These are the overflow and rounding branches, where a fault in a client's integer code would show first. Separately, on MegaETH and HyperEVM the block producer is closed and eth_call runs a replica, so mined transactions are the only evidence about the code that writes blocks, and cycle 24 counted which jump sides the producers executed but not which operand edges. Task 1: build one table of all 774 sides: for each, whether it was run by script sets 1 to 6 (research/network-risk/opcodes/coverage.json), by the cycle 25 cases, by the cycle 26 cases, and by mined transactions of each closed producer (the cycle 24 producer coverage in research/network-risk/cycles/024). Mark every side that nothing has run. For each of those say, from the bytecode and src/, whether it is unreachable by construction (give the argument: the bound that an earlier check enforces) or reachable. Task 2: for every reachable side that nothing has run, and for every math side that only one set has run, write a case that reaches it through the public interface (initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap, donate with chosen prices, liquidity and amounts; use the cycle 25 driver in research/network-risk/cycles/025/theme-unexecuted-sides.work). Where a side needs values no pool can hold, say so. Run the cases on all 21 networks through eth_call with state overrides at the real PoolManager address, bracketed by web3_clientVersion, compare every word with pyevm.py and with Ethereum, and check each swap against the exact-fraction rule of the cycle 25 checker. On Monad also run them through the compiled harness and say which results rest on a harness with the code-buffer fault that cycle 26 found. Task 3: operand edges. For each arithmetic site of the build list the edge operands that matter: SAR by 255 and SIGNEXTEND of a negative tick (src/libraries/TickMath.sol:61-63), SDIV and SMOD of a negative compressed tick (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:20-26), mulmod(a, b, not(0)) with a nonzero high word (src/libraries/FullMath.sol:24-33), the round-up mulmod of mulDivRoundingUp (FullMath.sol:112), DIV by a divisor above 2^128, SHL and SHR by 96, 128 and 192, MUL that wraps, SUB that borrows across all four limbs, BYTE at index 31, and SLT and SGT on values of opposite sign. In the traces of mined MegaETH and HyperEVM PoolManager transactions that cycles 23 and 24 saved, count how many frames reached each site with each edge operand. Where the saved traces lack stack values, fetch struct logs for a sample of mined swaps with negative ticks and large liquidity from the public endpoints, within their limits. List every site and edge that no mined frame of a closed producer has used. Task 4: for each edge that no mined frame has used on MegaETH or HyperEVM, say whether the replica's eth_call answer is the reference word (the earlier sets) and what it would take for the producer to differ from its replica: read in mega-evm at the tag behind mega-reth v2.3.1 and in the HyperEVM archive client whether any instruction handler is specialised by operand value, gas level or call depth.

code.title: Who can be the caller of the PoolManager and what it can be made to call on each network
code.task: The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes), research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python, research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/v4math.py is a transcription of the math libraries, research/network-risk/opcodes/jumpmap.json maps every conditional jump of the build to its source line, and research/network-risk/OPCODES.md holds what is already tested and read, with sections on what cycles 10 to 26 added and a list of what is not covered. Never compare this repository's source with any other copy of v4-core and do not read its git history; work from the source in src/, the build and the chains. Read-only RPC only, no transactions. Do not install software. Python 3, rustc 1.97 with cargo, go 1.24, node and the system C and C++ compilers are present, and you may compile downloaded source inside your own work directory. Keep downloads and build output under a directory named build/ or dl/ inside your work directory. Do not download compiler toolchains or other binaries to run them; source archives are fine. Record every sampling seed, save every mismatch record in full, and bracket each batch of calls to a public endpoint with web3_clientVersion so the build that answered is known. If an endpoint refuses your client (HTTP 403, 429 or a challenge page), record that and use another public endpoint; do not try to get around the refusal and use no API keys. Analysis only: no exploit code and no transactions. Lead L-1129, widened to all 21 networks. The PoolManager keys everything a user owns by msg.sender: currency deltas inside unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and the _accountDelta calls), ERC-6909 claims (src/ERC6909.sol), operator approvals, and liquidity positions (owner in the position key, src/libraries/Position.sol). So the CALLER opcode is a security boundary, and each network adds transaction types and system rules that decide what CALLER is. In the other direction, an ordinary account can make the PoolManager call any address in three fixed shapes: take of the native currency sends value with empty calldata to a recipient the caller names (src/types/Currency.sol:42-60), take of any other currency calls the currency address, which the caller also names, with transfer(address,uint256) (Currency.sol:61-95), and sync calls balanceOf(PoolManager) on it by STATICCALL (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). Hook calls reach any address a pool creator names with the hook selectors (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:132-150). Each network has system contracts and precompiles that act for their caller. Task 1, CALLER: for each of the 21 networks list every way a frame can run with a msg.sender for which no key signed and whose code made no call. Cover at least: deposit transactions and L1 to L2 address aliasing on the OP Stack networks, Celo and X Layer; retryable tickets, unsigned L1 messages and ArbOS internal transactions on Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium; HyperEVM system transactions (the archive client classifies a legacy transaction with gas price 0 as a system transaction and takes the sender from the s value: read that rule and the producer-side statement of it, and check in the blocks since the MRB fork that every such transaction's sender is a HyperCore system address); Tempo's account transaction type with batched calls, key authorisations, fee payers and sub-blocks; EIP-7702 delegation on every network that has it; Monad, MegaETH, Arc, BNB Chain, Polygon and Avalanche system transactions and system calls made around user transactions; and any precompile that forwards a call with a caller chosen by its input. For each: can an ordinary account choose the sender, and can the sender ever equal the PoolManager, a router, or an address that holds claims or positions? Test what can be tested read-only: eth_call and eth_estimateGas with from set to the PoolManager and with gas price 0, on each network, recording what the endpoint accepts (an eth_call accepts any from, so say what that does and does not prove). Task 2, transient storage across calls of one transaction: on networks where one transaction carries several top-level calls from different parties (Tempo batches, ERC-4337 bundles through the EntryPoint, the X Layer gasless carriers of finding F-151, sequencer-built bundles), the synced currency and reserves that sync leaves in transient storage (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol) outlive the call. Enumerate what a first party can leave behind for a second party in the same transaction (a synced currency that makes a native settle revert with NonzeroNativeValue at src/PoolManager.sol:356, a stale reserve that changes what the next settle credits) and whether any of it moves funds or only fails a call. Confirm on each network by eth_call with a small driver that transient storage is cleared between transactions and not between calls, including after a reverted frame. Task 3, callee: for each network list the system contracts, predeploys and precompiles (the lists in the network profiles and research/network-risk/networks.json, plus each network's documentation). For each address, what happens when the PoolManager is the caller of (a) a value call with empty calldata, (b) transfer(address,uint256) with chosen arguments and no value, (c) balanceOf(address) by STATICCALL, and (d) each hook selector with the hook calldata? Look for any answer that does more than move the caller's own payout: one that registers, delegates, stakes, bridges, withdraws, burns or blocks in the name of the PoolManager, that changes a balance the PoolManager holds for other users, that returns a balanceOf larger than what the PoolManager can transfer, or that returns success for a transfer it did not make (the PoolManager treats an empty return from an address with code as success, and Currency.sol:61-95 decides what it does for an address without code: read it and state it). Run the four shapes by eth_call with from set to the PoolManager against every such address on every network and record the result and the state change the trace shows where traces are served. Task 4: for every case where the PoolManager's balance of a currency can rise without a matching transfer by the caller (a system credit, a rebase by a system contract, a refund, a reward), state whether the rise can fall between a sync and a settle of an ordinary account and so be credited to it, and whose funds those are. Keep to network-level mechanisms; token issuer features are recorded elsewhere.
